en: Is it then that there is no liberation elsewhere than this?
No, there is not. What is the reason?
Because they are settled in a false view of a self;
for they do not determine that the designation "self" applies merely to the continuum of the aggregates.
What then?
They falsely imagine a self to be a distinct substance, and all afflictions arise from this grasping at a self.
But how is it known that this designation "self" applies only to the continuum of the aggregates (*skandha-saṃtāna*) and not to some other referent?
Because there is an absence of both direct perception and inference [to establish such a thing].
For those phenomena that exist, there is direct perception of them when no obstacle is present,
such as in the case of the six sense objects and the mind;
and there is also inference.
For example, as in the case of the five sense-faculties. In this regard, the following inference applies:

when a cause is present, it is observed that in the absence of another necessary cause, the effect is absent; yet when [that other cause] is present, the effect occurs, just as in the case of a sprout.

Furthermore, even when the object has come into range and attention—the cause—is present, the non-apprehension of the object is observed in cases such as the blind and the deaf, whereas its apprehension is observed in those who are not blind or deaf.
Therefore, in that case as well, the absence and presence of another cause are determined;
and that which is this other cause is the sense-faculty (indriya). This is the inference.
And since the self does not exist in this manner, there is no self;
however, as for the fact that the Vātsīputrīyas maintain that the *pudgala* exists,
that must first be examined.
Do they assert [it] as a substantial entity (*dravyataḥ*) or as a conceptual designation (*prajñaptitaḥ*)?
And what is this "substantial entity," and what is a "conceptual designation"?
If it is a distinct entity like form (*rūpa*) and so forth, then it is a substantial entity.
If it is a composite like milk and so forth, it exists as a designation (*prajñapti*).
What follows from this?
First, if it were to exist substantially (*dravyataḥ*), [then...]
Because its nature would be distinct [from the aggregates], it must be stated to be other than the aggregates, just as the aggregates are distinct from one another;
furthermore, its cause must be stated,
or else it must be unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Therefore, there would be the consequence of falling into the views of the non-Buddhists (tīrthika), as well as the fault of being purposeless.
If, on the other hand, [the person exists] by way of designation (prajñapti),
we also say the same.
For it exists neither as a substantial entity (*dravyataḥ*) nor even as a conceptual designation (*prajñaptitaḥ*). What then?
The person (*pudgala*) is designated in dependence upon the internal, appropriated, and present aggregates (*skandha*).
We do not understand this blind statement whose meaning has not been clarified.
What does "having appropriated" mean? If its meaning is that it is characterized by the aggregates, then it follows that the designation of a person (pudgala) applies only to those very aggregates.
Just as, depending upon form and so forth, the designation "milk" is applied to those very things; or, if this meaning is that [the person] depends upon the aggregates,
because the aggregates are the cause for the designation of a person.
That very same fault remains;
it is not designated in that manner.
How then? Just as fire is designated in dependence upon fuel.
And how is fire designated in dependence upon fuel?
For fire is not designated without fuel, nor can fire be designated as something other than fuel, nor as something non-other.
If it were other, then the fuel would be without heat.
If they were non-different, that which is to be burned would itself be the burner.
Likewise, the person (pudgala) is not designated apart from the aggregates (skandhas),
nor can it be asserted as different from the aggregates, because that would entail the consequence of eternalism.
Nor is it non-different, because that would entail the consequence of annihilation.
Come now, tell me first: what is fuel and what is fire?
From that, we shall understand how fire is designated in dependence upon fuel.
What is there to be said here? That fuel is the object to be burned and fire is the burner?
In this regard, precisely this must be stated: what is the object to be burned and who is the burner?
For in the world, wood and the like that have not yet caught fire are called "fuel" and "the object to be burned."
Fire is blazing and burning;
for that which is radiant, hot, and intense is what causes it to ignite and burn,
by bringing about a transformation in the continuity [of fuel].
Both of these consist of eight substances, and fire arises in dependence upon that fuel,
just as curd arises in dependence upon milk or vinegar arises in dependence upon honey;
therefore, it is said that [fire] exists "having taken up" (upādāya) the fuel.
Furthermore, it would be other than those [aggregates] because it exists at a different time.

And if this person (pudgala) arises in dependence upon the aggregates, it follows that he is both other than them and impermanent. Alternatively, if in that very same burning wood and so forth, the heat is considered to be fire, and the three co-nascent primary elements are considered to be the fuel; [then the same fault applies].
The distinctness of these two is also established by the difference in their characteristics;
however, the meaning of "depending on" (upādāya) must be explained:
how is it that fire is designated depending on that fuel?
For that [fuel] is neither the cause of that [fire], nor is it the cause of its designation;
for fire alone is the cause of its designation,
whether the meaning of "derived" (upādāya) is the sense of support, or the sense of coexistence.
In this way, it follows that the aggregates would be the support and co-existent factors of the person; thus, their distinctness is clearly asserted.
And in the absence of those [aggregates], the absence of the person follows, just as there is an absence of fire in the absence of fuel.
As for what was said: "If fire were other than fuel, the fuel would be non-hot"—what indeed is this that is called "hot"?
If it is heat itself, then the fuel is certainly non-hot, because its intrinsic nature is different from that [of heat].
Now, if it is argued that just as heat exists [in fire],
something else besides that fire which is hot by nature is established as hot through its conjunction with heat,
then there is no fault in their being distinct.
Furthermore, if all that— the burning wood and so forth— is accepted as both the fuel and the fire,
then the meaning of "depending upon" (upādāya) must be explained;
moreover, it follows unavoidably that the aggregates themselves are the person (pudgala), resulting in their non-difference.
Therefore, this is not established:

that just as fire is designated in dependence upon fuel, so too is the person (pudgala) designated in dependence upon the aggregates (skandhas). Furthermore, if it cannot be said that this [person] is other than the aggregates, then it follows that one could not say: "The objects of knowledge are fivefold: past, future, present, unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), and the inexpressible (avaktavya). Thus, it would be impossible to speak in such a way.

Indeed, it cannot be said that this [person] is a fifth category distinct from the past and so forth, nor can it be said that it is not a fifth category. Furthermore, when a person (*pudgala*) is designated, is it designated by apprehending the aggregates (*skandha*), or rather the person itself?
If it is by apprehending the aggregates, then the designation of the person would apply to those very aggregates themselves.
Because the person (*pudgala*) is not perceived;
otherwise, how could there be a designation of this person based upon the aggregates (*skandha*)?
For it would follow that the person itself is the very basis of that designation.
Now, if it is thought that the person (pudgala) is perceived when the aggregates (skandhas) exist, and therefore its designation is said to be based upon the aggregates;
then, since form (rūpa) is also perceived when the eye, mental attention, and light exist, its designation must likewise be said to be based upon them.
Furthermore, as with form, the distinctness of the person [from the aggregates] would be evident.
First, this must be stated:
by which of the six consciousnesses is a person (pudgala) to be cognized?
It is said: by all six.
How so?

If one discerns a person in dependence upon forms cognizable by the eye, that person should be said to be cognizable by the eye, but it should not be said whether he is the forms or not. Likewise, up to: if one discerns a person in dependence upon mental objects cognizable by the mind, that person should be said to be cognizable by the mind, but it should not be said whether he is the mental objects or not.
In that case, it follows that [the milk] would be identical to milk and so forth.

If one perceives milk or water by depending on visible forms cognizable by the eye, then it should be said that the milk or the water is "cognizable by the eye," but it should not be said whether they are "visible forms" or "not visible forms.
Likewise, it should be said that they are "cognizable by the nose, tongue, or body," but it should not be said whether they are "tangible objects" or "not tangible objects."
Lest there be the undesirable consequence of milk and water being [reduced to] four [distinct entities],
it is therefore established that just as milk or water is designated based on the collection of form and so forth, so too is the person (pudgala) designated based on the aggregates (skandhas).
As for what is said— that one discerns a person in dependence upon forms cognizable by the eye— [this is merely a conventional designation].
What is the meaning of this statement?
Does it mean that visible forms (*rūpa*) are the cause for the perception of a person (*pudgala*), or rather that one who perceives visible forms also perceives a person?
If visible forms are the cause for the perception of a person, then he [the person] must not be said to be other than them.
If that is the case, then form (*rūpa*) also should not be said to be something other than light, the eye, and attention (*manaskāra*),
because these are the causes for its perception.
Or, if one perceives a person (*pudgala*) while perceiving forms?
Does one perceive [the person] by means of that very same perception, or by means of another?
If it is by that very same [perception], it follows that the person has a nature non-different from form, or else the designation "person" applies to form itself.
And how is it understood that this person consists of form?
If it cannot be discerned in this way,
how can it be asserted that both form exists and the person exists?
For its existence is asserted by virtue of its being perceived;
this should be stated in the same way for all phenomena up to the dharmas.
Otherwise, because it is perceived at a different time, it would follow that [the self] is something other than form.

Just as blue and so forth cannot be said to be either identical to or different from yellow, and as one moment cannot be said to be either identical to or different from another moment, so it should be stated for all phenomena.
Furthermore, the identity or difference between the perception of form and the person who perceives it must likewise be left unexpressed.
In that case, it would follow that even regarding the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it is inexpressible; thus, there is a contradiction with the established doctrine (*siddhāntabheda*).

Furthermore, if this [person] exists but cannot be said to be either "the forms" or "other than the forms," then why did the Blessed One say: "Form is not-self, up to and including consciousness is not-self"?
By means of which visual consciousness this person (*pudgala*) is apprehended:
does that [consciousness] arise in dependence upon visible forms, or rather upon the person, or upon both?
If it arises in dependence upon visible forms, [then...]
It will not be able to cognize a person (pudgala), just as it cannot cognize sound and so forth.
For whatever object arises in dependence upon which visual consciousnesses arise, that alone is its objective condition (ālambana-pratyaya).
Now, does consciousness arise in dependence upon the person, or in dependence upon both?
This contradicts the Sūtra. For it is determined in the Sūtra that the arising of consciousness occurs in dependence upon a duality:
"In this way, O Bhikṣu, the eye is the cause and visible forms are the condition for the arising of visual consciousness."
For what reason?
Because, O monk, whatever visual consciousness there is, all of it arises in dependence upon the eye and visible forms;
thus, it follows that the person (pudgala) is likewise impermanent.
For it is stated in the Sūtra: “Whatever causes and whatever conditions there are for the arising of consciousness, those too are impermanent.
Now, if the person (pudgala) is not its object (ālambana), then it cannot be cognized by that [consciousness].
Furthermore, if it is asserted that the person is cognizable by the six consciousnesses, [then this follows].
Because it is cognizable by auditory consciousness, it follows that form is distinct from sound, just as sound is;
because it is cognizable by visual consciousness, it follows that sound is distinct from form, just as form is.
This same logic should be applied to the others as well.
Furthermore, this scriptural passage would be contradicted:
"O Brahmin, these five faculties have different ranges and different objects; each experiences its own respective range and object, and one does not experience the range and object of another."
Namely: the eye-faculty, the ear-faculty, the nose-faculty, the tongue-faculty, and the body-faculty.
The mind experiences the range and domain of these five faculties, and the mind is their point of reliance. Or rather, the person (*pudgala*) is not the object.
If it is not an object, then it cannot be cognized.
If that were so, it would follow that the mental faculty (*manaindriya*) is also non-deviant [in its operation].
For it is stated in the *Ṣaṭprāṇakopama-sūtra*: "These six faculties have different ranges and different objects; each seeks out its own respective range and object."
In this context, it was not stated by taking the [physical] sense-faculty itself as the faculty;
for it is impossible for the five [physical faculties] to have a desire for seeing and so forth, nor for their respective consciousnesses.
Therefore, here, by virtue of its predominance, the mental consciousness-faculty is what is intended and spoken of as the faculty.

Furthermore, that mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) which is governed solely by the predominance of the mind does not thus desire the objects of the other [senses]; therefore, this fault does not apply.

And it was said by the Blessed One: "O monks, I shall teach you the Dharma-discourse on 'all that is to be directly known' (*sarvābhijñeya*). Having said this, he spoke of the eye as to be directly known, visible forms, eye-consciousness, eye-contact, and whatever internal [feeling] arises conditioned by that eye-contact.
Whatever is felt— whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant, up to that which is conditioned by mental contact—

this is called the discourse on the Dharma regarding all that is to be directly known and fully understood. Therefore, it is determined that only this much is to be directly known and to be understood, and not a *pudgala*.
Therefore, this [person] is not even an object of cognition (*vijñeya*),
because wisdom (*prajñā*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) have the same objective domain.

Furthermore, those who maintain the existence of a person (*pudgalika*), seeing with the eye that "we see a person," fall into a position of false view (*dṛṣṭisthāna*), thinking, "We see the self by means of what is not-self."
And this has been definitively established by the Blessed One in the Sūtra:
“The person is designated only in relation to the aggregates,” as stated in the *Mānuṣyaka-sūtra*.
“Dependent upon the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of these three is contact; born simultaneously with contact is [feeling].”
Feeling, perception, volition—these four formless aggregates, together with the eye-faculty and form, are what is called "humanity.
Herein, there is this designation: "sentient being," "man," "human," "mānava," "nourisher," "person," "individual," "living soul," and "creature.
Herein, there is this claim: "I see forms with the eye."

In this regard, the conventional expression is as follows: "That venerable one had such a name, such a birth, such a clan, such food, such an experience of pleasure and pain, such a long life, such a duration of stay, and such a limit to his lifespan.
Thus, monks, all this is merely a designation and merely a conventional expression.
All these phenomena are impermanent, conditioned, and dependently originated.
The Blessed One has stated that a sūtra of definitive meaning (nītārtha) is the refuge;
therefore, it is not to be further scrutinized.
And thus it was said: "O Brahmin, 'everything exists' refers only to the twelve bases (āyatana)."
If this person (*pudgala*) is not a sense-field (*āyatana*), it is established that he does not exist.
But if he is a sense-field, then he is not "inexpressible" (*avaktavya*).

For those who see it in this way, [the Buddha said]: "To the extent, monk, that there is the eye, and to the extent that there are forms—in detail, to that extent, monk, the Tathāgata designates everything and all designation."

And it is said in the *Bimbisāra-sūtra*: “‘Self, self,’ O monks—this is how the ignorant, unlearned worldling, following after mere designations, [speaks]. But herein there is no self or anything belonging to a self; rather, it is this suffering that, as it arises, comes into being,” and so forth in detail.
Also, by the Arhatī Śailā, addressing Māra, it was said:
“Do you think ‘being’ (*sattva*) exists? For you have fallen into the view of Māra.”
This heap of conditioned formations is empty; no sentient being exists here.
"For just as the designation 'chariot' is used based on a collection of parts,
so too, based on the appropriation of the aggregates (skandhas), a 'sentient being' is spoken of by way of conventional truth.
Furthermore, in the *Kṣudrakāgama*, it is said concerning a poor brahmin:
Listen with respect, O Svādara, to the Dharma that releases all knots:
how the mind becomes defiled and how the mind is purified.
For the self itself does not exist for the self; it is imagined through perversion.
Herein, there is no sentient being or self; there are only these phenomena together with their causes.
Having reflected upon all these twelve factors of existence— the aggregates, sense-bases, and elements— a person (pudgala) is not to be found.
"Behold the internal as empty; behold the external as empty.
Even that one who cultivates emptiness is not to be found.
Thus it is said: "There are five disadvantages in the apprehension of a self."
There arises the view of a self and the view of a sentient being;
one becomes indistinguishable from the non-Buddhist outsiders;
and one has entered upon a wrong path.
"His mind does not enter into emptiness, does not become serene toward it, does not abide in it, and is not liberated;
the noble dharmas do not become purified for him.
Yet they do not accept this passage as authoritative.
What is the reason?
"Because this is not recited in our school (nikāya).
But do they take their own school alone as authority, or rather the word of the Buddha?
If the school alone is the authority, then the Buddha is not their teacher,
nor are they followers of the Son of the Śākyas.
On the other hand, if the word of the Buddha is the authority, [then the school is not the authority].
Why is this text not considered authoritative?
Is it because it is said that "this is not the word of the Buddha"?
What is the reason for this?
"The statement that 'it is not recited in our school' is an improper position. What is the impropriety here?"

For if a text is recited in all other schools and does not contradict the Sūtras or the nature of reality (dharmatā), to claim that it is not the word of the Buddha simply because we do not recite it is mere recklessness.
Furthermore, do they even lack this Sūtra: "All phenomena are without self"?
It might be thought [that they do].
For indeed, the person (pudgala) is not said to be a phenomenon (dharma), nor is it something other than a phenomenon.
If that is so, then it cannot be established as cognizable by the mental consciousness (manovijñāna);
for it is a fixed rule that the arising of consciousness occurs in dependence upon a dyad.

And here it is analyzed as follows: “To perceive what is non-self as self is a perversion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*), a perversion of mind (*citta-viparyāsa*), and a perversion of view (*dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa*).

This perversion consists in perceiving a self in what is non-self, but not in perceiving a self in a self. Furthermore, [it is said]: “The aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) are not the self. As for what was stated previously—that one should not say “they are form” or “they are not form”—that is indeed beyond reproach.

And it is said in another Sūtra: "O monks, whatever ascetics or brahmins regard anything as a self, they all regard only these five aggregates of clinging. Therefore, every instance of grasping at a self is [in fact] directed toward what is not-self. Likewise, it is said: "Whatever individuals have recollected, did recollect, do recollect, or will recollect their manifold former abodes, they all recollect only these five aggregates of clinging."
If this is so, why did he say, "I was possessed of form in past time"?
This is intended to demonstrate that those who recollect in such various ways [do not perceive a self].
However, if one were to perceive a person (*pudgala*) as possessing form, it would follow that they hold the view of a real body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
However, your [position] would not be a refuge at all because it is not found in the scriptures.
Therefore, the person (*pudgala*) exists as a conceptual designation (*prajñaptisat*), like a heap or a stream.
If that were so, then it would follow that the Buddha is not omniscient.
For there is no mind or mental factor whatsoever that could know everything,
because of their momentariness; rather, it is the person (pudgala) who knows.
If that is the case, then by admitting that the person (pudgala) does not perish when the mind perishes, its permanence would be admitted.
However, we do not declare the Buddha to be omniscient because of the simultaneous presence of all knowledge at all times;
what then?
By implication, that continuum which is called "Buddha" possesses this capacity: that by mere application of attention, non-erroneous knowledge arises regarding whatever is desired.
And it is said in this regard:

Because it possesses capacity through its continuum, just as fire is considered to be all-consuming, so too should the omniscient one be accepted, because of his knowing everything— not by knowing it all at once.
How is this understood?
Because of the mention of the past and so forth:
"Those Perfectly Awakened Ones who have passed away, those Buddhas who are yet to come,
and he who is the Perfectly Awakened One now— the destroyer of the sorrow of many."
Furthermore, you maintain that only the aggregates (skandhas) belonging to the three time periods exist, and not a person (pudgala).
If the aggregates themselves are the person, why did [the Buddha] say this:
"O monks, I shall teach you the burden, the taking up of the burden, the laying down of the burden, and the bearer of the burden"?
Why should this not be said?
For it is not logical that the burden itself should be the bearer of the burden.
What is the reason?
"It is not seen thus" [is the objection];
however, even the position that it is "inexpressible" (avaktavya) is not tenable.
What is the reason?
For it is not seen in this way;
moreover, it would follow that even the taking up of the burden (*bhārādāna*) would not be included among the aggregates (*skandha*).
It was for this very reason that the Blessed One taught the bearer of the burden (*bhārahāra*).
“Whoever that venerable one is, of such a name, who has remained for such a long time, and whose life-limit was such”—this [person] is intended to be understood in this way;
let him not be understood otherwise as being either eternal or ineffable.

Furthermore, it is the aggregates themselves that lead to the affliction of the aggregates—namely, the preceding ones leading to the subsequent ones—and thus, having designated them as the "burden" and the "bearer of the burden," they were so spoken of.
For a burden is indeed that which has the sense of being oppressive.
There certainly exists a person (pudgala), because it was said: "To say 'there is no spontaneously born being' is a false view.
And who says such a thing as "there is no spontaneously born being"?
We state in the *Mānuṣyaka-sūtra* that the Blessed One has analyzed the sentient being (*sattva*) exactly as it exists.

Therefore, for one who denies the continuum of aggregates (*skandha-saṃtāna*) designated as a "spontaneously born sentient being" in the next world, this is a false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), namely: "There is no spontaneously born sentient being. This is because the aggregates themselves are what are spontaneously born.
Now, if this wrong view were one that denies the person (*pudgala-apavādikā*), by what means would it be abandoned?
For it is not logical that it should be abandoned either through seeing (*darśana-heya*) or through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),
because the person is included within the category of sentient beings (*sattva*).
If it is argued that [the person] is not the aggregates because of the statement, "A single person arises appearing in the world," we say no;
for the designation "one" is applied even to a collection, as in the cases of "one sesame seed," "one grain of rice," or the singular expression "one heap.
Alternatively, the person must be called "conditioned" (saṃskṛta), since you admit that it possesses the quality of arising.
It does not arise in the same manner as the aggregates, by way of a previously non-existent manifestation;
rather,
it arises through the appropriation of other aggregates.

Just as one says "a sacrificer is born" or "a grammarian is born" due to the acquisition of knowledge; "a monk is born" or "a wandering ascetic is born" due to the assumption of a [particular] mark (liṅga); and "one who is enlightened is born" or "one who is diseased is born" due to the assumption of a different state.
It is not because of a general rejection; for indeed, it was rejected by the Blessed One in the *Paramārtha-śūnyatā-sūtra*:

"Thus, O monks, there is karma and there is its maturation, but an agent is not found—[an agent] who casts off these aggregates and reconnects with other aggregates, except for the conventional designation of phenomena (*dharma-saṃketa*)."
And it is said in the *Phalgusūtra*: "I do not say that 'one appropriates' is a trivial matter.
Therefore, there is no appropriator of the aggregates, nor is there any one who casts them off.
Furthermore, what kind of person does your reverence believe to be a sacrificer, or even one who is ill?
If he takes the person (pudgala) as the example,
that is unestablished; if, on the other hand, he takes the mind and mental factors (citta-caitta), [the same fault applies].
No;
for them, there is only the arising of something entirely new at every moment.
Or, [if you mean] the body:
The same applies to that [person] as well;
and just as in the case of the body, knowledge, and the marks, it follows that the aggregates (skandhas) and the person (pudgala) are distinct.
Thus, what is aged is simply another body, and likewise what is diseased.
For the Sāṃkhya doctrine of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*) has been refuted;
therefore, these [arguments] lack a valid example.

Moreover, if the arising of the aggregates (*skandha*) is not admitted as being prior to that of the person (*pudgala*), then it is clearly demonstrated that he is both distinct from them and eternal.

By one who asserts that the five aggregates constitute a single person, how is their distinctness not being asserted? For instance, although there are four primary elements (*bhūta*) and yet matter (*rūpa*) is one, matter is not something other than the primary elements.
This fault applies only to one side of the argument.
In which position?
In the position that there are only the primary elements (*bhūtamātra*).
Nevertheless, just as form is merely the primary elements, it follows that the person (*pudgala*) is accepted as being merely the aggregates (*skandhamātra*).

If the person (*pudgala*) is merely the aggregates (*skandha*), why did the Blessed One not declare whether that life-principle (*jīva*) is the same as or different from the body? It was because he took into account the intention of the questioner; for the latter had asked with reference to a single substantial life-principle, an internal agent (*antarvyāpārapuruṣa*).
And since that [self] does not exist anywhere, how can its difference or non-difference [from the aggregates] be explained?
It would be like the hardness or softness of a tortoise's hair.
Furthermore, this very point has already been resolved by the predecessors.
The Elder Nāgasena was approached by King Kaliṅga, who said to him:
"I would like to question the Venerable One; however, monks are often talkative.
If you would answer exactly what I ask, then I shall question you."
Being told, "Ask," he asked:
"Is that soul the same as this body, or is the soul one thing and the body another?
The Elder replied, "This has not been declared."
He said:
"Venerable sir, was it not previously made a formal promise to you that nothing else should be spoken?
Why then has this other thing been said—that this is undeclared?"
The Elder said:
"I too would like to question the Great King; however, kings are often talkative.
If you would answer exactly what I ask, then I shall inquire."
Being told, "Ask," he asked:
"Regarding that mango tree in your inner apartments, are its fruits sour or are they sweet?
He replied, "There is no mango tree at all in my inner apartments."
"Was it not previously made known to the Great King by me that he must not speak anything else?
Why has this other thing been said, namely, 'there is no mango tree at all'?
He replied, "How can I declare the sourness or the sweetness of the fruits of a tree that does not exist?"
In the same way, O Great King, that very *jīva* does not exist; how then could I declare its difference from or non-difference from the body?
Why did the Blessed One also not say that it simply does not exist?
Because he had regard for the disposition of the questioner.

For he would perceive the non-existence even of that continuum of aggregates which is designated as a "living being," and thus would fall into a false view due to his ignorance of dependent origination; moreover,
he is incapable of receiving such a teaching.
For this reason as well, this is determined to be so:

because the Blessed One said, "Ānanda, if, when asked a question by the wanderer Vatsagotra, I were to answer that 'the self exists,' would that not be inconsistent with my teaching that all phenomena are without self? And Ānanda, if, when asked a question by the wanderer Vatsagotra, I were to answer that 'the self does not exist'... [Vatsagotra would be...]
The wandering mendicant, already deluded before, would fall into even greater delusion, thinking: "I had a self, but now it no longer exists.
Ānanda, to say "the self exists" leads to the extreme of eternalism; Ānanda, to say "the self does not exist" leads to the extreme of annihilationism—this is the detailed explanation.
And it is said elsewhere:
"Considering the fangs of [wrong] views, the destruction [of roots of virtue], and the loss of [wholesome] actions,
the Jinas teach the Dharma like a tigress carrying her cub."
"For one who has accepted the existence of a self would be pierced by the fangs of [wrong] views;
failing to reach conventional reality, he would cause the destruction of the ship of virtue.
Thus it was said again.
Because it does not exist, the Blessed One did not describe the living being as either identical to or different from the aggregates;
nor did he say that it does not exist at all, lest even the conventional designation be rendered non-existent.
For in whichever continuum of aggregates there is the existence of the fruits of good and evil,
that [continuum] would not be called "the living being," because it is taught that no living being exists.
He did not even say that the "living being" among the aggregates is a mere designation;
for at that time, such people were incapable of realizing emptiness.
For instance, when asked whether the self exists or does not exist, he did not say "it certainly exists";
rather, out of consideration for the questioner's disposition, why would he not have said "it exists" if it were indeed so?
The non-explanation regarding whether the world is eternal and so forth is also due to consideration of the questioner’s intention.
For if the self were intended by him as "the world," then because that [self] does not exist, a fourfold explanation would be improper.
Alternatively, if the entire cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) were intended as "the world," for that too it would be improper.
If the world were eternal, no one would attain parinirvāṇa.
If the world were eternal, no one would attain parinirvāṇa. If the world were non-eternal, there would be annihilation for all.
If it were both ways, then by necessity some would attain parinirvāṇa while others would not;
if it were neither way, then neither parinirvāṇa nor non-parinirvāṇa would be attained.
Therefore, because parinirvāṇa depends upon the path, no definitive determination is made in any of these four ways, just as in the case of the sparrow belonging to the Nirgrantha disciple.
For this very reason, there is no categorical explanation regarding the fourfold set beginning with "the world is finite.
Indeed, this fourfold set has the same meaning;
for instance, after the wandering mendicant Muktika had asked that fourfold set, he further asked: "Does the entire world depart by means of this path, or only a portion of the world?"
The Elder Ānanda said: "Muktika, you are now asking the very same question that you first asked the Blessed One, though by this different method. Thus it is with all [the questions].
Even the tetralemma regarding whether the Tathāgata exists after death was not answered because of the intention of the questioner;
for he asked having identified the liberated self as the Tathāgata.

But one who maintains that the person (*pudgala*) is a real entity should be questioned: "For what reason does the Blessed One declare that the person exists while living, yet does not declare it after death?
[If you say] "Because [otherwise] the fault of eternalism would follow," then why does he declare: "Maitreya, in a future time you shall become a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha"?
And for what reason does he prophesy the rebirth of a deceased disciple who has passed away, saying, "So-and-so has been reborn in such-and-such a place"?
For even in this way, there would be the consequence of eternalism (*śāśvatatva*).

Furthermore, if the Blessed One, having previously seen a person, no longer sees them after they have entered final nirvana (*parinirvṛta*) and thus does not prophesy because of ignorance, then either the Teacher’s omniscience must be called into question, or it must be admitted that such a person does not exist at all.
Then, even if it is not explicitly stated, it follows that he exists and is eternal;
this being established, one need not even say whether he sees or not.
If that is so, then let this also be made gradually indeterminate: whether the Blessed One is omniscient or not.
The person (pudgala) certainly exists, because it is stated that "there is no self in me" is a point of view (dṛṣṭisthāna),
and "it exists" is also stated to be a point of view;
therefore, this [argument] is not a proof.
However, the Abhidharmikas maintain that both of these are included within the view of grasping at extremes—the views of eternalism and nihilism;
and this is indeed logical, because it is stated in the Vātsya-sūtra: "Ānanda, to say 'the self exists' leads to eternalism; Ānanda, to say 'the self does not exist' leads to nihilism."
If, then, there is no person (pudgala), who is it that transmigrates? For it is not logical to say that "transmigration itself transmigrates.
And yet, the Blessed One has said: "Of beings shrouded by ignorance, who run on and transmigrate..."
Now, how does a person transmigrate? By means of abandoning one set of aggregates and taking up another.
This position has already been answered.

Just as it is said that a momentary fire "migrates" by means of its continuity (*saṃtati*), so too the collection of aggregates (*skandhasamudāya*) designated as a "sentient being," which is characterized by craving and grasping (*tṛṣṇopādāna*), is said to "migrate. If this is merely the aggregates, why did the Blessed One say, "At that time, on that occasion, I myself was the teacher named Sunetra"?
Why should he not have said so?
Because the aggregates are distinct [from it].
Now, what is the person?
It is that very same thing.
For [if that were so], he would be eternal.
Therefore, by saying "I am indeed that," he demonstrates the continuity of a single stream,
just as one says, "That same fire has come burning."
If the self were to exist, only the Tathāgatas would perceive it clearly.
And for those who perceive it, grasping at a self and affection for a self would become even firmer.
Furthermore, because of the statement in the Sūtra, "When there is a self, there is what belongs to a self," their grasping at a self would operate even more intensely toward the aggregates.
This would be the view of a self-existent body (satkāyadṛṣṭi).
And when there is the view of "mine," there is attachment to what belongs to the self.
Thus, for those whose bonds are thoroughly consumed by an even firmer attachment to self and "mine," liberation would become exceedingly remote.

Now, if it is thought that affection does not actually operate toward a self, then what kind of logic is this—that affection arises through the conviction of a self in what is not-self, yet does not arise toward a real self?
Therefore, this tumor of false views has arisen within this teaching: namely, the grasping at a person (pudgala) by some, and the grasping at the non-existence of everything by others.
Furthermore, for those non-Buddhist teachers who consider the self (*ātman*) to be a distinct substance, the fault of the impossibility of liberation remains unshakable.
If, then, the self does not exist in any way whatsoever, how is it that there occurs the recollection or recognition of an object experienced long ago within momentary states of consciousness?
[It occurs] from a particular state of consciousness (*cittaviśeṣa*) which follows upon the conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) of the object of memory.

From what kind of specific state of mind does memory arise immediately thereafter? It arises from a specific state of mind that possesses an application [of attention] (*ābhoga*) similar [to the original perception], as well as notions (*saṃjñā*) and so forth related [to it], and whose power has not been impaired by a particular physical basis (*āśraya*), grief, distraction, or the like.

For even such a specific state of mind is incapable of producing that memory if it does not belong to that same continuum; and conversely, even if it belongs to that same continuum, a different kind of state of mind is incapable of producing that memory.
However, the memory arises that "it is capable" precisely because capability is not observed in anything else.
But how then does one mind remember what was seen by another?
For if that were so, the mind of Yajñadatta would remember what was seen by the mind of Devadatta.
Not so, because there is no connection.
For there is no connection between those two, such as the relation of cause and effect, as there is between two [moments] belonging to a single continuum.
Nor do we say that one mind remembers what was seen by another.
Rather, from the mind of seeing, another mind of recollection arises through the transformation of the continuum (saṃtatipariṇati), as has been explained; what fault is there in this being so?
Furthermore, recognition arises precisely from recollection.
If there is no self, who is it that remembers? What is the meaning of "remembers"?
It means that one grasps the object by means of memory.
What is that apprehension other than recollection?
Who, then, performs the recollection? That which performs it has been explained: it is a particular state of mind that serves as the cause of recollection.
As for the statement that "Caitra remembers," it is said that "Caitra remembers" because one observes that memory arising from the continuum designated as "Caitra.
If there is no self, whose is this memory?
For what purpose is this genitive case?
It is for the sense of ownership;
as in, "Who is the owner of what?"
For example, Caitra [is related to] a cow.
How is he its owner?
Because the employment of the cow for carrying, milking, and so forth is dependent upon him.
Furthermore, where is memory to be employed, such that its master is sought in this way? It is to be employed toward the object to be remembered.
For what purpose is it to be employed?
It is for the purpose of recollection:
"Ah, how well-spoken are the words of those nurtured in happiness!
Indeed, that very [happiness] ought to be employed for that purpose."
And how should it be applied?
Is it by way of production, or by way of dispatching?
It is by way of production, because of the impossibility of the movement of mindfulness.
In that case, it follows that the cause alone is the master and the fruit alone is the property;
for the cause has sovereignty over the fruit, and by means of the fruit, the cause possesses it.
Indeed, this [memory] belongs only to that which is its cause.

Furthermore, that continuum of the collection of conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*) designated as "Caitra," which is grasped as a single unit and called the "owner" of the cow, is so designated by taking into account its causal role in the production of modifications in other locations; however, in reality, there is no such single entity named Caitra, nor is there any such thing as a cow.
Therefore, even in that case, there is no relationship of owner and owned apart from the state of being a cause.
The same should be said regarding such questions as "Who cognizes? and "Whose is the cognition?
The distinction is this: its causes are the sense faculty, the object, and attention, as applicable.
As for the one who says that because an action (*bhāva*) depends upon an agent (*bhavitṛ*), every action indeed depends upon an agent—
just as in the case of "Devadatta goes," where the action of going depends upon the goer, Devadatta;
so too is consciousness (*vijñāna*) an action.
Therefore, one who says "there must be someone who cognizes" should be asked:
"Who is this Devadatta?"
If it is the self that is the object of proof, then it is precisely that [self] which must be established.
If, on the other hand, it is the person of conventional usage, even he is not some single entity; for those very conditioned factors (saṃskāra) are what are designated by such a name.
In this regard, it is as with Devadatta walking or as with him cognizing. How does Devadatta walk?

Conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are indeed momentary; however, because their continuum is uninterrupted, they are grasped by the foolish as a single mass of a sentient being called "Devadatta. When these [phenomena] act as the cause for their own continuum to appear in another location, it is said that "Devadatta walks."
And that arising in another location is what is called "motion," just as the terms "goes" and "going" are applied to a series of flames or sounds.
Furthermore, it is those very [moments] of consciousness, while acting as causes, that are said to be "Devadatta knows."
Even the Noble Ones speak of them in that way by way of conventional designation for the sake of communication.
As for what was stated in the Sūtra, "consciousness cognizes," what does consciousness do there?
It does nothing at all.
Just as it is said that an effect conforms to its cause—
even though it performs no action— because it acquires its own nature through similarity;
in the same way, consciousness is said to "cognize."
Because it acquires its own nature through similarity, even though it does nothing at all.
But what is its similarity? It is the state of having that [object's] form.

For this very reason, it is said that what arises even from that sense faculty cognizes the object, not the sense faculty itself. Alternatively, here too, because the continuum of consciousness serves as the cause for cognition, the statement "consciousness cognizes" is faultless, since the term for an agent is applied to the cause— just as one says, "the bell rings."
Furthermore, just as one says "the lamp goes," so too one says "consciousness cognizes.
And how does the lamp go?
The term "lamp" is applied metaphorically to the continuum of flames.
Just as one is said to "go" to a certain place when arising in other locations,
so too consciousness is metaphorically designated as a continuum of mental states;
when it arises with respect to different objects, it is said to "cognize" that object.
Just as in the case of the statement "form is born" or "form abides," where the agent of becoming is not distinct from the act of becoming itself, so it would be for consciousness as well.

If consciousness arises from consciousness and not from a self (*ātman*), why does it not always arise as exactly the same [as its predecessor], and why does it not arise according to a fixed sequence like a sprout, a stalk, and a leaf?
This is because change while persisting (*sthityanyathātva*) is a characteristic of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*).
For this is the very nature of the conditioned: that there must necessarily be a transformation within the continuum.

Otherwise, in the case of those absorbed in meditative concentration at will, since the arising of similar body and mind would be indistinguishable from the first moment, there could be no subsequent emergence from it on one's own.
Furthermore, the sequence of moments of consciousness is indeed strictly determined.
Because it arises from that very source from which it ought to arise;
for even things of an identical form may be capable of producing [an effect],
due to a distinction in their lineage (*gotra*).

For example, if immediately after a woman’s mind there arises a mind that reviles her body, or a mind directed toward her husband, son, and so forth, and then later, through the transformation of the continuum (*saṃtati-pariṇāma*), a woman’s mind arises again, it is capable of producing either that mind which reviles her body or that mind directed toward her husband, son, and so forth.
Because it belongs to that same lineage;
otherwise, it would not be capable [of arising].
Furthermore, if various kinds of mind have arisen in succession from a female mind, then whichever is more frequent, more recent, or more proximate will arise again.
Because that cultivation is more powerful,
except for a specific external bodily condition occurring at that time;
why does that very same powerful cultivation not always bear fruit?
Because alteration (anyathātva) is a characteristic of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*), and because that alteration is conducive to the arising of the fruit of another cultivation;
this [explanation] is merely a brief indication regarding all types of mind.
However, mastery over the knowledge of uninterrupted causes belongs only to the Buddhas.
For thus they say:
"The causes for every single aspect of even one eye of a peacock's feather cannot be known by those who are not omniscient; for that knowledge is the power of the Omniscient One."
This is even more so for formless mental states.

However, this objection clearly applies to that particular non-Buddhist who believes that the arising of consciousness originates from a self: "Why does [consciousness] not always arise in exactly the same way, and why does it not follow a fixed sequence like a sprout, a stalk, and a leaf?
If he were to argue that this is because [consciousness] depends on specific conjunctions with the mind (*manas*), we say: no.
Because conjunction with anything else is unestablished;
furthermore, since the definition of conjunction is explained as "the attainment of two conjoined things preceded by non-attainment," it would follow that the self is limited in size.
Consequently, from the movement of the mind, there would follow either the movement of the self or its disintegration.
If it is argued that there is conjunction with a specific part [of the mind], we say no; for it is impossible for that very [mind] to possess such a part.
Or, even if such a conjunction were to exist, how could there be a distinction in the conjunction when the mind is eternal and undifferentiated?
If it is argued that [the cognition] depends on a particularity of the intellect (*buddhi*), that very point is what must be questioned: how does this particularity of the intellect arise?
If it is argued that it arises from the contact of the self and the mind (*ātma-manas-saṃyoga*) depending on a particularity of the formative impressions (*saṃskāra*), [then...]
Let it be from the mind alone, because it depends upon specific conditioning factors (*saṃskāra-viśeṣa*);
for no capacity whatsoever is perceived in a self, just as the "phuḥ svāhā" of a quack doctor is not perceived in the accomplishment of a medicinal effect.
If it is argued that there is a conjunction of those two [mind and effort] when a self exists:
It is a mere word.
If you say that it is the basis,
then what is the basis of what?

For it is not logical that those [mental factors] are supported by it as a painting or a jujube fruit is supported [by a wall or a bowl], nor is it logical that it is their support as a wall or a bowl is [the support for what is placed upon it].
Because of the fault of being subject to resistance (*pratighātin*), it cannot be a support in that manner.
How, then, is it?
If you say that it is like the earth [being the basis] for odors and so forth,
we are thoroughly satisfied!
For this very point is our proof that there is no self.
Just as earth is not something other than its odor and so forth—
who indeed could distinguish an earth that is separate from its odor and so forth?
The designation "the odors and so forth of the earth," however, is for the purpose of specification.
For it is only those specific [entities] designated as "smell" and so forth that are perceived in that way, and not others—
just as the term "body" is applied to a wooden statue.
Furthermore, even though there is a dependence on specific conditioning factors (*saṃskāra*), why does the simultaneous arising of all cognitions not occur?
For that which is the strongest among them constitutes the obstruction of the others;
why does that very strongest [cause] not always produce its fruit? Let that which is the principle governing this [case] be the same for cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
If it is argued that the self is postulated as something useless,

yet the self must necessarily be admitted because memory and other such phenomena belong to the category of qualities (*guṇa*), and because a quality must necessarily reside in a substance (*dravya*) by its very nature, and because these [qualities] cannot have anything else as their substratum— [we reply: no.

For it is not established that these are the category of quality (*guṇa*); rather, everything that exists for us is substance (*dravya*), according to the statement: "The fruits of the ascetic life are six substances."
Nor is it established that these [qualities] reside in a substance;
for the meaning of "residence" has already been examined.
Therefore, that [argument] is merely something trivial.
If the self does not exist, for what purpose is there the undertaking of action?
It is for the purpose of thinking, "May I be happy; may I not be suffering.
But who is this so-called "I" which is the object of this ego-conception?
The aggregates are its object.
How is this known?
Because of attachment to them.

However, because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with cognitions such as "fair-skinned," this ego-consciousness (*ahaṅkāra*) is observed to be coreferential with cognitions such as "I am fair-skinned," "I am dark," "I am fat," "I am thin," "I am old," and "I am young. And these modes are not observed to belong to the Self (*ātman*).
For this reason as well, it is understood that "this [person] exists within the aggregates.

Just as there is a metaphorical designation of "self" (*ātma-upacāra*) with respect to the body—which is actually a benefactor of the self—as in the expressions, "This very person is I," or "This very person is my servant," there is a metaphorical designation of "self" even toward a benefactor; however, this is not the actual *ahaṃkāra* (the conceit of "I").
If the body is the objective support (*ālambana*), why does [the conceit of "I"] not also have another's body as its objective support?
Because there is no connection [between the self and anything else].
For this ego-conception arises only with respect to that which is connected to it— whether body or mind— and not elsewhere,
due to such habitual practice throughout beginningless saṃsāra.
And what is the relationship?
It is the relationship of cause and effect.
If the self does not exist, to whom does this "I-conceit" (ahaṅkāra) belong?
This brings us back to the question: "For what purpose is this genitive used?
It means that this [result] belongs to whatever is its cause.
And what else could be the cause?
It is a faulty mind, permeated by prior ego-grasping, which takes its own continuum as its object.
If there is no self, who is it that is happy or miserable? [Who is it] in whose basis pleasure or pain has arisen?
Just as one says "a tree has flowered" or "the forest has borne fruit," what,
then, is the basis for these two?
It is the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana).
It has been stated according to how it was established:
if there is no self, who is the agent of these actions, and who becomes the experiencer of their fruits?
What is the external referent of this term "agent"?
One who acts is an agent; one who enjoys is an enjoyer. These are synonyms; there is no difference in meaning.
"An agent is one who is independent"—thus do the experts on definitions state the definition of an agent.
Furthermore, independence with respect to a particular action does exist for someone;
this is observed in the world in the case of Devadatta regarding bathing, sitting, walking, and so forth.
Furthermore, who is this Devadatta that you cite?
If it is the self, then that very thing is yet to be proven. If it is the five aggregates, then those very things are the agent.
This action is threefold: action of body, speech, and mind.
Among these, regarding bodily action first: the activity of the body is dependent upon the mind;

the activity of the mind with respect to the body is likewise dependent upon its own causes, and those [causes] are also [dependent] in the same way. Thus, there is no independence for anything whatsoever.
For all entities proceed in dependence upon conditions;
and since even a self, being independent, is admitted to be a non-cause, its independence is not established.
Therefore, no agent characterized in such a manner is ever perceived.
That which is the primary cause of something is called its agent;
however, no causality whatsoever is observed in the case of the self.
Therefore, even in this sense, it is not logical for it to be an agent.

For desire is born from mindfulness; discursive thought is born from desire; from discursive thought comes effort; from effort comes the vital air; and from that comes action. What does the self do here?
Furthermore, what is this "enjoyment" of the fruit for which this self is imagined as an enjoyer while performing [actions]?
If it is argued that it is "perception," [we reply:]...
The self has no capacity for apprehension, because that has been refuted in the case of consciousness.
If there is no self, why is it that the accumulation of demerit and merit does not occur without a sentient being as its locus?
Because feeling and so forth have no basis [other than these], and their basis is the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), not a self; this has already been explained.
If there is no self, how can the production of a fruit in the future arise from an action that has perished?
And even if a self exists, how can the production of a fruit in the future arise from an action that has perished?
[The answer is: It arises from merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) which are based upon it.
Just as the answer has already been given to the question "What depends on what?", this same logical principle applies here.
Therefore, let the result arise from dharma and adharma themselves, even though they are without a substratum.
We certainly do not claim that the production of a fruit in the future arises from a karma that has already perished.
What then?
[It arises] from a specific transformation of that continuum, like a seed and its fruit;
just as it is said that a fruit is produced from a seed.
And it does not arise from a seed that has already perished, nor does it arise immediately [after the seed];
what then?
Because of a specific transformation in its continuity (*saṃtati-pariṇāma-viśeṣa*), which is produced through the sequence of sprout, stalk, leaf, and so forth, ending with the flower;
and because that [fruit] is produced from the flower, why is it called the fruit of that seed?
For it is by that [seed] that a supreme capacity has been imparted to the flower.
For if it were not preceded by that [action], it would not be capable of producing such a fruit;
thus it is said that the fruit arises from the action.
Yet it does not arise from an action that has already perished, nor does it arise immediately [afterward].
What then?
It is from a specific transformation of that continuum (*saṃtati-pariṇāma-viśeṣa*).
But what is the continuum, what is transformation, and what is the specific [transformation]?
That which is a continuous flow of successive moments of consciousness preceded by karma is a "continuum" (*saṃtati*); its arising in a different state is "transformation" (*pariṇāma*).

Furthermore, that [moment] which is immediately capable of producing a fruit is a "specific transformation" (*pariṇāmaviśeṣa*), because it is distinguished by being the final [stage] of the transformation.
For example, the death-consciousness accompanied by grasping (*sopādāna*) [is the cause] of renewed existence.

Even though [the manifestation of karma] is preceded by three types of action, that karma which is heavy, or proximate, or habitual, or that which was performed—its efficacy is manifested, and not that of another.
And it is said:
"That which is heavy, that which is proximate, that which is habitual, and that which was performed..."
In the cycle of saṃsāra, karma ripens first for that which is earliest.”
In this regard, the capacity to yield a ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*), which was established by the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*), ceases once it has given its ripened fruit.

However, the capacity to yield a concordant fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*), which was established by the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), ceases in the case of afflicted states upon the arising of their antidote;
in the case of non-afflicted states, it ceases when one attains final nirvana due to the absolute cessation of the mental continuum.
Now, why does one maturation (vipāka) not produce another maturation, just as one fruit produces another fruit from a seed?
First of all, everything is not identical to the example;
for even in that case, it is not from the fruit itself that another fruit is produced.
What then?
[It arises] from a specific transformation born of a specific state of softening.
For that particular mode of the primary elements which brings about the sprout there is its seed, and nothing else.
However, by means of a future designation or because of similarity, even the preceding continuum is called a "seed.

Likewise here as well, if from that maturation (*vipāka*) there arises a transformation of the mind—whether wholesome-with-outflows (*sāsrava-kuśala*) or unwholesome (*akuśala*)—produced by specific conditions such as hearing the true or false Dharma, then from that [transformation] another transformation arises and not otherwise; thus this is the same.
Or rather, it should be understood in this way:

Just as from a citron flower dyed with lac juice, a red filament is produced in the fruit arising from a specific transformation of the continuum (*saṃtati-pariṇāma-viśeṣa*), yet no further [red filament] arises from that one; so too, from a maturation born of karma, no further maturation arises.
This has been shown according to its gross features as accessible to our intellect.
However, that "continuums perfumed by various karmas distinguished by diverse potencies have reached such a state and produce such a fruit" is the domain of the Buddhas alone.
It has indeed been said: "No one other than a Buddha can, in every respect and with certainty, discern karma, its cultivation, the attainment of its activity, and from that, the fruit."
Having heard this nature of the Dharma in the teaching of the Buddhas, which is purified by well-established causes and paths,
[one sees] those who are blind, engaged in various activities of wrong views.
Having cast aside the doctrines of the heretics, those who are not blind proceed [to liberation].
For this selflessness is the sole path to the city of Nirvana, radiant with the rays of the Tathagata-sun’s words, and traversed by thousands of noble ones.
One with weak vision does not see it, even when it is wide open.
Thus, this has been taught as merely a mere indication for those of excellent intelligence,
like the site of a wound through which poison spreads by its own power.
The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, the Treasury of the Person, is completed.
This is the work of the venerable master Vasubandhu.
Of those phenomena that arise from causes, the Tathāgata has declared their cause, as well as their cessation; such is the teaching of the Great Śramaṇa.

This is the religious gift of the venerable Śrīlāmāvāka, a scholar from the Northern Region and a bearer of the entire teaching of the Tathāgata in the most excellent Mahāyāna. Whatever merit is herein, etc.
May there be auspiciousness!
